title: New sessions at the top — and the foot takes your colour
description:
New sessions now land at the top of the sidebar. Where a launch landed used to depend on where you were standing — appended at the bottom of the list, and quietly nested into whatever group held your selection — so the tab you had just asked for was the one you then had to go and find, and the group you were reading in became the group your next session joined. It is the first row now, at the top level, whatever was selected: from the launcher, from ⌘T/⌘N/⌘I/⌘U, from ⌘⇧A. A session joins a group by being launched from that group's own **+**, which puts it at the top of that group, and a newly launched pinned group lands at the top too. Two things deliberately unchanged: a **duplicate** still appears directly under its original, because it is about that row rather than about new work, and **dragging** a tab onto a group still drops it at the bottom — a hand aiming at a group is placing the row itself.

The “Clave by Antasphere” mark stands clear of the traffic lights. It used to start 16px past the last of the three macOS buttons, the same gap as the window's own gutter, so it read as crowded up against them rather than as its own thing; it starts 22px clear now — a nudge, not a step. And it stays put when you step into **Settings** or **Extensions**, which used to open with a bare spacer where the mark had been. Nothing moves in fullscreen, where there are no buttons and the mark already sits in the gutter, and on Windows and Linux it takes that same gutter instead of holding clearance for buttons that are not there.

The sidebar's foot wears your own colour. That panel is made of your Antasphere field, and its controls were still lighting up in the app's grey — which over a coloured ground reads as dirt on the picture rather than as a control waking up. Every control in the foot now takes its hover from your palette's own signature hue, a colour already in that palette, instead of the grey used everywhere else in the app. The panel also gained the 3px inset the rest of the system has: a row exactly one control tall in a box with no padding had its button sitting on the card's border, reading as a block cut out of the card rather than as something inside it.

title: Both edges of the window, reworked
description:
The sidebar is reworked end to end, and the side panel opposite it now speaks the same language.

Dragging a session works the way the hand expects. A drag carries the row under the cursor and nothing else — clicking a group header selects every row in it, so dragging any one row used to empty the whole group into the drop target and delete it. Every row offers a top and a bottom half, so the first and last position of another group can be aimed at; from inside, a group's header means "first position"; and a row's own place always means "stay", so changing your mind mid-drag no longer moves the row out. Rows of a collapsed group stop catching drops meant for the group underneath. The drop line itself is drawn over the seam between rows and takes no space at all — it used to be a slot inserted into the list, so every time it moved the rows lurched under a cursor that had not moved. When the line snaps to a new row the trackpad gives the same quiet tick Finder uses, so the hand feels the target change without the eye leaving what it is dragging.

A group header no longer lays every terminal's icon out in a row that ran off the sidebar past a handful, truncating the group's name first. It carries one terminals button showing how many are attached, lit in a running terminal's colour, which opens a panel listing each one with its icon, command, folder and a running dot — click to start or focus, right-click to edit, New terminal at the foot.

Typing in the group switcher now shows you what Enter will do: the first chip left standing takes the state hovering it gives, so the key you are about to press has a visible target instead of being a guess you confirm by pressing it. Cmd+F reaches the field again — the shortcut had been aiming at an attribute the rebuilt field no longer carried, so it opened the sidebar and focused nothing. The chip row collapses when it holds no chips instead of keeping a line open to announce that the panel is empty. And the list below no longer dies against the switcher: the cards scroll behind it, and with nothing between them they slid up into its bottom border, which made the panel read as the first row of the list rather than as the chrome the list runs under. There is now the same 4px that holds the launcher and the switcher apart, closed by a hairline.

At the bottom, three rows of different shapes — a feedback card, a work tracker, a bare user button — become one panel, cut from the same cloth as the launcher and the switcher above, so the list is bracketed by chrome at both ends instead of trailing off. Its ground is the Antasphere generative field, and your avatar is that field at full strength with the glyph knocked out of it; Settings offers a painted swatch per palette and a redraw, because no hex describes a field. The second line stops counting minutes worked and starts answering "can I keep going": your tightest usage window as percent left, with a meter that drains. Nothing names a cap — which ones an account has is the service's business — so it takes whatever came back and shows whichever is closest to stopping you.

Files and Git are under one chrome now. The bar on top carries what belongs to both tabs — the folder the panel points at, collapse-all, help — instead of one copy per tab, and under it each tab brings its own: the search field for Files, the git controls for Git. The repo tree draws its rules at the head of a block, at the depth of the row that opens it, so a folder holding repos is ruled between its folders rather than under every repo inside them. And "N repos — live updates paused" stopped being a warning strip across the top of the list you came to read: a big tree is a fact about the folder, not a fault, so it is a folded footnote at the foot of the panel with the current limit, a refresh, and one button that opens the setting.

Inside the Git tab, orange leaves the two places it least belonged. A file you changed and a commit waiting on the remote are the normal life of a repo, and painting both as warnings meant a healthy repo showed a wall of them. Modified takes the app's own accent, incoming a plain informational blue, and green, red and blue keep their conventional meanings. Orange survives on exactly one row — a file that an incoming change and your working tree both touch — so the one real heads-up reads. A repo's files sit on the same row height as the file tree above them, the blocks inside a repo have air between them, and the vertical indent guides came down to about a third of their old weight: repeated once per level on every row, at a border's strength they read as a table's gridlines rather than as a guide.

title: Several windows — the whole app, as many times as you like
description:
Clave can run in several windows at once. A window is the app once more: put it on whatever workspace you want — the same one as another window included — and work there. File › New Window (⌘⇧N) opens one on the workspace you are looking at, and every workspace row in the toolbar switcher has an Open in new window action. Tabs and groups live in the window you opened them in, and that is all a window means: your sidebar in each window is its own, and every window comes back at the next launch on its workspace, at its size and place, with its groups and sessions.

Right-click a tab or a group for Move to window… — the tab keeps its id and its scrollback (tmux-backed sessions only; a plain terminal stays where it is). Closing a window kills nothing: its tabs and groups land in the first window. Switching a window's workspace touches nothing else.

Agents got the same reach: clave_open_session, clave_create_group, clave_launch_group and friends take a window to land in, clave_open_window opens one, clave_move_session moves a tab across windows, and clave_list reports the windows and which one holds each tab.

For anyone running Clave's own test suite: test instances no longer appear on screen at all.

title: One surface language, from the sidebar to the menus
description:
The sidebar's top controls are a panel now, cut from the same cloth as the toolbar and the terminal cards — same border, same surface, same height, and a top edge that lines up exactly with the first card beside it. The buttons inside dropped their pill fills: the panel already frames them, so the row reads as hairlines and hover states instead of loose chips on a bare field.

Under it, a new group switcher. It lists the groups you have running, with All to come back to everything, and a search field that widens it to every group the workspace knows about — including the ones declared in .clave or auto-discovered from your tree that are not running yet. A group the search finds but that is not started appears under the results as a closed card with a Start button, so reaching a group you have not opened no longer means leaving the sidebar for the picker dialog. Chips wrap instead of scrolling sideways.

The list itself has room to breathe: taller rows, larger icons, more padding. Groups behave properly too — hovering a group's header now lights the whole group in its own colour, and every control inside a coloured group takes that colour instead of a grey that never belonged there. A group's terminal icons stay readable when the group is not the one you are looking at, which is exactly when you need to see which of them is running.

The surfaces that float over the app caught up in the same release. Menus, popovers, tooltips and dialogs share one language: the panel's radius and border, quiet inset rows, and a single scrim in place of the three different ones that were in use. They also animate — the enter and exit classes they relied on came from a plugin that was never installed, so every menu used to teleport. The terminal grid keeps zero animation on purpose: appearing instantly is the point. If you have reduced motion switched on, every entrance collapses to a fast fade.

title: Software Update, where you can actually reach it
description:
Clave now has a Software Update pane in Settings and a Check for Updates… item in the menu bar — the two places a Mac app is supposed to keep them. The pane shows the version you are running, whether a newer one exists, when Clave last looked, and a Download & Install button with live progress.

This fixes a real way of getting stuck. The update notice used to be a banner pushed to the sidebar once, five seconds after launch and then every half hour. If you missed it, dismissed it, or the check quietly failed, nothing on screen would admit an update existed and there was no way to ask — which, since auto-update is how Clave ships, meant no way to upgrade. The app now holds that state and hands it over whenever the window asks, so the answer survives a restart.

When an update will not install, the pane stops being a dead end: a link to install the release by hand, and a link to the updater log that says why it failed. A download that dies mid-transfer also retries itself once before bothering you.

title: Views you declare, workspaces in the toolbar
description:
A group's page can now be declared in its .clave file rather than set by hand: a quick-launch terminal marked "groupView": true binds its server as the group's web view at launch, and a group-level "view" names a page that needs no process at all. Single sessions get the same thing without a group — an agent can attach a live dashboard to its own tab, which persists across restarts and starts again in one click. An untrusted .clave file never renders a page.

The workspace switcher moved to the toolbar: click the workspace name to see every workspace on this machine and switch with one click, and add one straight from the folder picker instead of a detour through Settings. The sidebar's pill row is gone.

In the git panel the change count is now a button like the sync arrows — click it to fold the local file list away and leave just what a pull or push would carry. Those sections get a spelled-out Pull (rebase) and Push back in their headers, a clean repo says so inside a contained field, and every list scrolls a little past its last row instead of ending flush.

Plus a pass over the things that shifted under you: tree rows no longer resize when a badge appears, dividers follow the tree's indentation, panels lost their drop shadow, and several buttons that were a few pixels off now line up.

title: A new git panel, a new launcher, less chrome
description:
The git panel is now your real folder tree: repos sit where they live on disk, single-child chains merge into one row, and folders fold with rolled-up change counts. The ↓ and ↑ badges are buttons — they unfold Incoming and Outgoing sections listing every file a pull will bring or a push will send, with a ⚠ on files you also changed locally. The commit bar is tucked behind the pencil icon.

Starting a session no longer asks where: the launcher is split into a terminal button and an agent button that remembers the agent you last used in that workspace, opens at the workspace root, and keeps a folder button for anywhere else. Groups carry their own prompt, so a group's + starts a session already briefed. And the launcher stays pinned instead of scrolling away.

Groups can also open as live pages — attach a dev server, a dashboard or an HTML file and clicking the group renders it instead of the terminals. HTML files render in their own tabs too, with a Rendered ⇄ Source toggle. Gone, because nobody used them: the Extensions entry and the toolbar's detected-URL tags. Terminals now reach the edges of their panes.

title: Server buttons in the toolbar
description: Give a quick-launch terminal a serverUrl and its button becomes a service switch: one click starts the server if needed and opens it in your browser, with a live status dot showing up, starting, or down.

title: Edit markdown right on the page
description: Page mode is now a Notion-style writing surface — click anywhere and type. Headings, lists and code blocks convert as you write, checkboxes toggle with a click, and ⌘S saves clean markdown back to the file.

title: Markdown opens as a page
description: Markdown files now render as a document-style page by default — a centered reading column with real typography, frontmatter hidden and its title on top. The compact preview and the source editor stay one click away via the new Page / Preview / Source switcher.

title: Agents can show you files and notify you
description: Agents in your tabs gained two new tools: clave_open_file opens a document they produced as a file tab for you to read or edit, and clave_notify sends a native notification when long-running work finishes in a tab you are not looking at — click it to jump straight there.

title: Spot Clave in Mission Control
description: When you open macOS Mission Control or App Exposé, Clave now covers its window with a blurred overlay and a large Clave mark, so you can pick it out instantly among the thumbnails. No extra permissions needed — toggle it under Settings → Appearance.

title: Antigravity CLI replaces Gemini CLI
description: Google retired the standalone Gemini CLI and folded it into the new Antigravity CLI. Cmd+I and the New session menu now launch the Antigravity CLI (the agy binary) with its brand mark. Your existing Gemini sessions, pinned groups, and .clave files keep working and reopen as Antigravity automatically.

title: Install plugins from Extensions
description: The Extensions view is no longer read-only — you can now manage plugins right inside Clave. Open a marketplace to install any plugin it offers or remove the marketplace, open an installed plugin to enable, disable, or uninstall it, and use Add marketplace to register a new one from a GitHub repo, git URL, or local path. Disabled plugins are flagged so you can tell them apart. Changes apply the next time you start a Claude session.

title: Trusted workspace folders
description: Adding a workspace folder now trusts it as a root, so every .clave file inside it opens without re-prompting — no more repeated warning dialogs when you run many workspaces or when a file gets rewritten. A new Trusted workspace folders card in Settings lists your trusted roots and lets you revoke any of them. Files opened from outside a trusted folder still ask for confirmation.

title: Browse your installed Extensions
description: A new Extensions view (under New Session in the sidebar) shows everything installed for a Claude Code profile. Browse your marketplaces as cards, drill into one to see its plugins, then open a plugin to see its skills, agents, commands, and MCP servers. A dedicated MCP Servers tab lists every server across all sources, and when you run multiple Claude accounts a profile dropdown scopes the whole view.

title: Anonymous usage ping
description: Clave now sends one anonymous ping a day — a random ID, the app version, and your platform, nothing else — so we know how many people use it. The exact payload is documented in the README, and a new Privacy section in Settings → General lets you turn it off with one click.

title: A redesigned Settings page
description: Settings is now a full page with its own sidebar — General, Appearance, and Usage — replacing the footer popup. Options are grouped into clean cards with slim controls, and the sidebar footer is a compact row whose gear takes you straight to Settings.

title: Agents can now drive Clave
description: A Claude session can open new agent tabs with an initial prompt and launch your pinned workspace groups through a built-in MCP server — so a coordinating agent can set up and hand off work across tabs. Agents can also request a secret without it ever showing in the chat: you review the action in the toolbar and paste the value into a masked field, scoped to that one action.

title: Git panel stays current in large folders
description: When a folder has many repositories, the Git panel pauses live polling — but it no longer goes stale silently. It now refreshes automatically when an agent finishes a turn or the window regains focus, shows the last update time with a refresh spinner, and a new Git section in Settings lets you change the pause threshold or turn pausing off entirely.

title: Run multiple Claude accounts side by side
description: Define Claude Code accounts in Settings, each pointing at its own config directory. With more than one, a picker appears when you start a Claude session and each session's header shows which account it's running under — so a work and a personal account can run in parallel without touching environment variables.

title: Sessions that survive quitting
description: Sessions now run inside tmux, so your agents keep going after you quit Clave, survive crashes, and reattach automatically next launch — reachable from any terminal via `tmux -L clave attach`. On by default when tmux is installed; toggle it in Settings → Sessions.

title: Live status on session tabs
description: Claude Code tabs now show their status at a glance: the icon pulses blue while working, an amber dot means Claude is waiting on your input, and a green dot flags a session that finished while you were away. Driven by Claude Code's own lifecycle signals, so it's accurate, not guessed.

title: Claude Agents sessions
description: Launch a `claude agents` session from the New session menu or with ⌘⇧A. A faint trailing glyph in the sidebar tells Claude Agents and skip-permissions sessions apart from plain Claude Code.

title: Redesigned agent conversations
description: The remote agent chat has a fresh look — your messages in clean rounded bubbles, agent replies as easy-to-read flowing text, and a refined composer with a circular send button.

title: Provider logos in the sidebar
description: Sessions now show their provider's real logo — Claude Code, Gemini, and Codex each display their brand mark in the sidebar, so you can tell them apart at a glance.

title: Edit files right in Clave
description: Files now open syntax-highlighted and instantly editable — just click into the code, type, and press ⌘S to save. Highlighting follows your theme, and markdown opens rendered with a Source toggle.

title: Templates launcher
description: Your .clave session templates now open from a folder-plus icon next to the Sessions header, in a searchable popover — so a long list of templates no longer crowds your sessions.

title: Codex CLI sessions
description: Launch OpenAI's Codex CLI from the New session menu or with Cmd+U, just like Claude Code and Gemini CLI.

title: Sidebar selection focus
description: Selecting a session, group, or file tab now fades the unselected rows so your active selection stands out at a glance.

title: Redesigned sidebar
description: A cleaner sidebar: New session and Queue as top tabs, your sessions under one Sessions header with pinned groups inline, consistent spacing and alignment from shared design tokens, and slightly less round corners across the app.

title: Publish Branch from the Git panel
description: Committing on a brand-new local branch now surfaces a Publish Branch button in the Git panel — it pushes the branch to origin with upstream tracking so your commits don't sit there invisibly.

title: Undo in the sidebar
description: Press Cmd+Z to undo the last sidebar action — disbanding a group, dragging a session, renaming, or recoloring. Up to 50 steps are remembered.

title: Windows Support
description: Clave now ships a Windows installer alongside every macOS release — Windows users can download a `.exe` setup directly from GitHub Releases

title: Model Pill
description: See the active Claude model at a glance in the terminal header — click for a popover with reasoning effort, thinking, fast mode, context window, and live session cost. Everything stays up to date via Claude Code's statusLine hook

title: Context Inventory
description: See what Claude Code loads into context per session — CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, MCP, hooks — with a live percentage badge, category breakdown, and estimated token cost

title: Open Git Diffs as Tabs
description: Double-click any changed file to preview, then open the diff as a persistent document tab — with live stage/unstage and right-click access from the git tree

title: Daily Cost Tracking
description: See exactly how much you spend per day, week, or month with the new cost bar chart on the Usage page

title: Activity Heatmap
description: Your Usage page now shows a full year of activity as a GitHub-style contribution heatmap

title: Smarter Work Tracker
description: Accurate wall-clock time tracking with concurrent session support, now integrated into the sidebar footer

title: Design System & Chat History
description: Unified design tokens across the app, and a new chat bubble layout for browsing conversation history

title: Work Tracker
description: Track your daily coding sessions, build streaks, and visualize weekly trends right from the sidebar
